title: Survey calculations
summary: How computers entered New Zealand survey and engineering work through coordinates, control networks and route calculations, while most maps remained on paper. Follows the shift from numeric output to reusable digital geometry.

sourceNotes.text: The date of the first stored-program government computer is disputed. Treasury’s IBM 650 was installed in 1960 and opened in March 1961; a later study argues that an ICT 1201 for Education may have entered service earlier. The chapter keeps that chronology qualified.

The Ministry of Works examples come from A. C. Shailes’s 1980 public-sector computing account. The Clutha Valley saving is a period estimate; the Mangaweka description reports a proposal-specific route method and cost context.
NZGD49 is a geodetic datum; NZMG is a projection based on it. LINZ’s geodetic history and technical guidance support the distinction and the cautions about historic transformations.
Russell Gladstone Dick’s 1966 “Maps and mapping” account distinguishes office staff who calculated survey records from the later use of electronic computers for demanding mathematics.
W. I. Reilly’s 1973 paper describes NZMG. Te Ara records the 1977 publication of the first NZMS260 sheet, T12 Thames.
A 1969 grid-survey contouring paper and a 1976 programme for irregularly spaced stadia field readings document early computer contouring.
